title: The Twisted History of Dentistry
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of dentistry from ancient times to the early twentieth century. They cover Babylonian toothworm beliefs and henbane remedies, Egyptian dentistry and the Papyrus Ebers, arsenic and other harmful treatments, Vedic twig-chewing and early dentifrices, Roman dental work including Celsus's lead fillings, and medieval tooth drawers and barber surgeons who also bled patients. They then discuss Pierre Fauchard as a pioneer of modern dentistry, the development of anesthetics (sleep sponges, ether, nitrous oxide, cocaine), the history of toothbrushes and toothpaste, George Washington's dentures, X-ray discoveries and the focal infection craze including Henry Cotton, and the rise of the American Dental Association and the scandalous Painless Parker. The episode closes with listener mail about a Pavement reference in the Salem witch trials episode.
topics: Henry Cotton New Jersey Lunatic Asylum

segments.title: Opening banter and research sources
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Josh's dental work and introduce the episode on dentistry history, thanking sources such as the British Dental Association, a Georgian blog, and a James Wybrandt book, and giving a trigger warning about painful historical procedures.

segments.title: Toothworms and ancient Babylon and Egypt
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Babylonian toothworm belief and henbane-beeswax smoke remedies, then move to ancient Egypt, Hesy-Ra as a early recorded dentist, and the Papyrus Ebers with treatments including opium, henbane, and arsenic.

segments.title: Chinese, Vedic, and Roman dentistry
segments.summary: The hosts discuss traditional Chinese medicine acupuncture points for toothache, Vedic texts recommending twig brushing and honey-oil dentifrices, and Roman dental work such as crowns, bridges, and Celsus's lead fillings, plus a Roman urine mouthwash.

segments.title: Middle Ages, tooth drawers, and barber surgeons
segments.summary: Dentistry declined in the Middle Ages. Physicians avoided teeth, leaving work to tooth drawers, who performed traveling circus-style extractions with bands and snake oil sales, and to barber surgeons, who also bled patients. Bloodletting for toothaches and leeches are discussed.

segments.title: Early dental tools, botched extractions, and Fauchard
segments.summary: The hosts describe dental tools like the pelican and dental key, a botched extraction recorded in 1770, deaths from infected extractions in London, and Pierre Fauchard as a pioneer who used armchairs and evidence-based methods and organized dental tools.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the anesthetics segment.

segments.title: Anesthetics history
segments.summary: The hosts trace pain relief from opium, hashish, and sleep sponges to ether, which Raymond Lull reportedly knew of in the 1200s, nitrous oxide and Humphry Davy's paradise bags, Horace Wells' failed demonstration, W. T. G. Morton's ether demonstration, and the introduction of cocaine as a local anesthetic by William Stewart Halsted.

segments.title: Toothbrushes, toothpaste, George Washington, and focal infection
segments.summary: The history of toothbrushes and abrasive toothpastes, the spread of brushing after World War Two, George Washington's dentures, and early X-ray findings that led to the focal infection craze, including Henry Cotton's extractions at the New Jersey State Lunatic Asylum.

segments.title: American Dental Association and Painless Parker
segments.summary: The founding of the American Dental Association and its efforts to distinguish itself from tooth pullers, with Edgar Randolph Painless Parker used as a scapegoat. The hosts mention a future short episode on the amalgam wars.

segments.title: Listener mail: Pavement reference
segments.summary: A listener named Alan Coleman points out a Pavement song about Increase and Cotton Mather, referenced in the Salem witch trials episode. The hosts read a verse and thank him.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and contact information for the show.
